tldr: A 3D generative world model that unifies diverse physical phenomena—including rigid bodies, elastoplasticity, granular media, and cloth—into a shared 3D particle and rigid-body representation, enabling long-horizon prediction and contact-rich planning via Flow Matching and Diffusion Forcing.
hero_caption: Overview of GPWM. Taking the ParticleWorlds dataset (6 domains, top) as input, a U-shaped multi-resolution spatiotemporal Transformer generates future motions of particles and rigid bodies via denoising. It reduces prediction error by an average of 31% over the best prior baselines, enabling physical simulation from images and contact-rich manipulation planning via search in latent noise space (bottom right).
overview:
For a robot to manipulate objects skillfully in unseen environments, it needs a world model that can predict how the physical world evolves and plan how to intervene to reach a desired state. While video generative world models have become popular, they only predict pixel-level appearance. They cannot directly handle accurate 3D physical contact or geometric changes. On the other hand, conventional 3D particle-based models are often specialized for a single material or are deterministic, making them prone to severe error accumulation over long horizons.

To address this, the authors propose GPWM, a generative particle world model that represents deformable and granular media via particle displacements and rigid bodies via spatial transformations, combined with Flow Matching and Diffusion Forcing. They built ParticleWorlds, a massive simulation dataset of 25.5 million frames, and successfully trained a single model with shared weights (Unified GPWM) spanning six physical domains: rigid bodies, elasticity, plasticity, granular media, and cloth.

Experiments show that both domain-specific models and the Unified model outperform prior methods by large margins, cutting prediction error by an average of 31%. Furthermore, by learning a generative prior over joint actuator and object motion, the authors introduce a new planning framework that searches the model's "latent noise space" rather than unconstrained action space. In tasks requiring complex contact sequences like pushing and picking—where standard action search almost completely fails—the plans execute open-loop in simulation and achieve goal-directed manipulation.
contributions: Proposed GPWM, a 3D generative particle world model that unifies rigid, deformable, granular, and cloth materials into 3D particle and rigid displacements, achieving long-horizon rollouts far beyond the training window (over 55x) via Diffusion Forcing.
Constructed ParticleWorlds, a 25.5-million-frame 3D physical simulation dataset spanning diverse geometries, physical properties, and robot embodiments (rods, parallel grippers, and dexterous hands).

Demonstrated superior prediction accuracy over prior baselines across all six physical domains (averaging a 31% error reduction), with a single Unified GPWM outperforming domain-specific baselines and even specialist models in two regimes.

Established a contact-rich manipulation planning framework via a generative interaction prior, generating joint actuator–object motions and solving complex contact tasks by optimizing in latent noise space.

sections.heading: Toward World Models That Generate Real 3D Physics Instead of Just Video Pixels
sections.summary: Physical world models for robotics must capture multi-material dynamics, contact, and long-term causality. Existing video models lack direct 3D spatial representation, while prior 3D particle models were deterministic and limited to single materials. GPWM breaks these limitations, enabling both diverse physical prediction and contact-rich planning with a single generative architecture.
sections.details:
Building a general-purpose physical world model requires handling diverse materials, predicting contact dynamics over long horizons without degradation, and assisting robot action planning. However, popular video world models only generate visual appearance rather than directly representing the 3D motion and physical contact of objects in space. On the other hand, learned physical simulators using 3D point clouds or particles exist, but most are deterministic predictors that only work over short horizons or specialize in a single material (such as only rigid bodies or only clay).

This paper asks: can we learn 3D particle motion with a generative model to capture diverse physical dynamics, predict over long horizons, and perform contact-aware planning?

GPWM (Generative Particle World Model) places all physical entities into a single unified representation by modeling deformables, cloth, and granular materials like sand through particle displacements, and rigid bodies through spatial rigid transformations. This stabilizes long-horizon predictions even in scenes with thousands of interacting particles, and it is designed to co-generate actuator motions (such as robot end-effectors) in the same geometric representation.

sections.heading: The Intersection of Learned Physics Simulators and Diffusion-Based Planning
sections.summary: Learned physics simulators are shifting from deterministic to generative models, but scaling and multi-material versatility have remained largely unexplored. Meanwhile, applying trajectory-based diffusion planning to contact-rich 3D manipulation faces challenges. GPWM combines both, leveraging multi-resolution processing and latent noise search to balance scale with search efficiency.
sections.details:
### Physics Simulators and Learned 3D Dynamics
Conventional learned simulators (such as GNS, ParticleFormer, and PGND) were primarily deterministic models specialized for a single domain. However, contact and friction involve inherent physical uncertainty with multiple plausible outcomes, causing deterministic models to produce blurry or physically collapsed trajectories. GPWM fundamentally differs by capturing rigid bodies, elastoplasticity, cloth, and granular materials as a unified generative distribution using a single architecture.

### Generative Dynamics and Long-Horizon Rollouts
The closest prior works to GPWM are PhysCtrl and PhysiFormer. However, they were trained only on fixed, short time horizons and fed the entire scene's point cloud directly into a Transformer, limiting their scale to small scenes of a few hundred points. In contrast, GPWM uses a multi-resolution architecture to scale up to 12,000 particles and integrates Diffusion Forcing to enable autoregressive streaming generation far beyond the training window.

### Generative Models for Planning
Methods like Diffuser have applied trajectory generation to reinforcement learning and planning, but extending them to contact-rich 3D physical environments remains challenging. Optimizing directly in action space often exploits predictive inaccuracies in the world model (out-of-distribution actions), yielding plans that fail when executed. By learning a joint distribution over object and actuator motions, GPWM gains the ability to search latent noise within a physically plausible interaction prior.

sections.heading: How Multi-Resolution Transformers and Diffusion Forcing Generate Physical Motion
sections.summary: GPWM represents deformables as particle displacements and rigid bodies as rigid transformations, processing them with a multi-resolution spatiotemporal Transformer. Combining Flow Matching with Diffusion Forcing and streaming generation with frame-wise noise levels, it achieves long-horizon physical prediction and contact-rich planning in latent noise space.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Particle and Rigid Body Representation
GPWM represents a scene as tracked particles and rigid bodies. For deformable particles ($N_p$ points), the generation target is the frame-to-frame displacement $\Delta\mathbf{P}_t^p = \mathbf{P}_{t+1}^p - \mathbf{P}_t^p$. Integrating displacements recovers absolute positions, providing translation invariance. For rigid bodies, to prevent geometric deformation, it predicts a 9-dimensional frame-to-frame rigid transformation $\Delta\mathbf{q}_k^t = [\Delta\mathbf{t}_k^t, \Delta\mathbf{r}_k^t]$ (translation and rotation). Robot actuators (grippers or end-effectors) are similarly represented as particles or rigid links, provided either as conditioning inputs or generated jointly with objects during planning.

### 3.2 Multi-Resolution Spatiotemporal Transformer
Computing full attention across thousands of particles causes an intractable quadratic computational cost. GPWM adopts a U-Net-style multi-resolution architecture. Anchor particles are selected via Farthest Point Sampling (FPS) from the densest level, and features are downsampled and aggregated into coarse levels using PointNet++-style local grouping. Inside the Transformer blocks, temporal attention across time and spatial attention within frames are factorized. Coarse levels capture global object-actuator interactions across the scene, and a decoder interpolates features back to fine particles.

### 3.3 Flow Matching and Diffusion Forcing
The model is trained with Flow Matching, but critically incorporates Diffusion Forcing, which assigns an independent noise level $\tau_t \in [0, 1]$ to each future frame. During training, this simulates states where near-term frames have low noise while distant future frames have high noise. Instead of directly predicting velocity vectors, the model adopts an endpoint parameterization that predicts clean clean displacements and rigid transformations, achieving stable convergence with a pure L2 loss without auxiliary physical loss terms.

### 3.4 Streaming Long-Horizon Generation
At inference time, GPWM performs streaming rollout: it sequentially denoises near-term frames until committed, shifts the context window forward by one step, and appends fresh Gaussian noise at the end. This allows rollouts over hundreds of frames without exploding errors while keeping the model's computational window fixed (e.g., 16 frames).

### 3.5 Planning with a Generative Interaction Prior
When trained to co-generate passive object trajectories and robot actuator trajectories, the model acquires a natural prior over physically plausible contact patterns. Given a sparse reward function targeting an object goal, the optimal noise is found by backpropagating gradients with respect to the initial noise vector $\mathbf{z}$ through the frozen world model (Latent Noise Optimization; LNO) or via sampling-based Noise CEM. Because the search is constrained to the learned interaction manifold rather than an unconstrained action space, the planner avoids unrealistic solutions.

sections.heading: ParticleWorlds: A Massive 25.5-Million-Frame Physical Dataset Across Six Regimes
sections.summary: To capture physical diversity, the authors created ParticleWorlds (25.5 million frames), covering rigid bodies, elastoplasticity, granular media, cloth, and various robot interactions. All data are standardized into a common particle and rigid-body format, with automated quality audits to filter out numerical instabilities and interpenetrations.
sections.details:
To comprehensively learn diverse physical phenomena, the authors constructed ParticleWorlds, a large-scale simulation corpus comprising 267,864 episodes and 25,463,677 frames.

The dataset consists of six domains:
- **Free Fall**: Blocks and complex shapes of elastic, plastic, and granular (sand) materials dropping, colliding, and deforming in the Genesis simulator.
- **Dragging**: Gripping, pulling, holding, and releasing parts of elastic and clay-like surfaces.
- **Garment Folding**: A two-finger gripper folding roughly 1,000 garments across 10 categories in the SIM1 environment (up to 10,000 particles).
- **Pushing**: Pushing blocks across a tabletop using a rod or parallel gripper.
- **Pick and Place**: Sourced from SkillWeaver, covering grasping and placement of single objects and objects in dense clutter.
- **Dexterous Hands**: Dexterous manipulation such as rotating cubes or turning screwdrivers using multi-fingered hands (XHand1, Sharpa).

All simulator outputs are converted into a shared representation of tracked particles and rigid transformations with consistent particle identities. Automated audit rules strictly screen out penetration, explosive particle scattering, and numerical divergence, retaining only high-quality physical trajectories.

sections.heading: Beating Baselines by 31% and Unlocking Contact Planning via Noise-Space Search
sections.summary: GPWM outperformed prior methods across all six domains of rigid, deformable, granular, and cloth dynamics, with a single Unified model even surpassing specialist models. It exhibited strong generalization to unseen shapes and material stiffness. In planning tasks, noise-space search solved pushing and picking where action-space search completely failed.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Predictive Performance Across Diverse Physical Domains
GPWM was evaluated against leading 3D dynamics models, including GNS, PGND, PointWorld, and PhysCtrl. GPWM outperformed the best prior baseline in each of the six physical settings, reducing prediction error by an average of 31% (e.g., from 53.0 mm to 40.0 mm in Free Fall, 7.8 mm to 6.1 mm in Dragging, and 23.9 mm to 13.3 mm in Pushing).
Notably, the single "Unified GPWM" trained across all domains with one set of weights beat prior baselines in 5 out of 6 domains. In Dragging and Pick and Place, it even surpassed the domain-specific specialist GPWM models. This confirms that vastly different physical regimes can share representations and positively cross-pollinate within a single model.

### 5.2 Generalization across Geometry, Material Properties, and Real Images
Generalization was tested in the Free Fall domain. Although trained on 1 to 4 objects, testing on unseen geometries with 5 to 7 objects (up to 7,168 particles) caused only a minor error increase from 37.5 mm to 45.2 mm (whereas PhysCtrl degraded significantly from 48.5 mm to 120.9 mm). Interpolating Young's modulus (stiffness) also resulted in less than a 2 mm increase in error.
Furthermore, in Real2Sim experiments—where 3D meshes reconstructed from single RGB images via SAM 3/3D and MoGe-2 were converted into particles and fed into GPWM—the model successfully predicted realistic, natural collisions and collapses.

### 5.3 Planning via Generative Interaction Priors
Task success (Task Progress from 0 to 1) was evaluated on three contact-rich manipulation tasks: Pushing, Pile Manipulation, and Picking. Baselines included Action CEM optimizing displacement space using the same GPWM or PointWorld.
The results were stark. In Pushing (which requires navigating around an obstacle) and Picking (which requires precise grasping and lifting), Action CEM achieved task progress below 0.01 (near total failure). In contrast, Latent Noise Optimization (LNO) and Noise CEM achieved high progress rates of 0.40 to 0.57. Because discovering precise contact timings and approach paths through random action proposals is nearly impossible, searching along the model's learned natural interaction prior provided a decisive advantage.

captions.F3: Physical prediction from a single RGB image (Real2Sim). Real-world objects (toy car, bell pepper, lemon, ball) are segmented and reconstructed into 3D meshes from images, assigned material properties (elastic, sand, clay), and dropped; GPWM accurately predicts realistic collisions and deformations.
captions.F5: Planning with a generative interaction prior. By optimizing latent noise (LNO) toward a goal (green cross), the model autonomously generates a sophisticated contact trajectory where the actuator lifts an object over an obstacle wall.

sections.heading: Moving Past Full State Tracking and Toward Fast Online Control
sections.summary: GPWM currently relies on fully tracked 3D particles and known object identities as inputs. Future work will also address negative transfer in unified multi-domain learning and the heavy computational overhead of backpropagating through diffusion steps during planning.
sections.details:
Several clear challenges remain:
- **Integration with Perception**: The current setup assumes fully tracked 3D particle states. Building an end-to-end pipeline that reconstructs particles and object IDs directly from raw RGB/RGB-D video is an important next step.
- **Specialist vs. Unified Gap**: Although Unified GPWM is remarkably strong, it still trailed specialist models in certain domains. Adopting Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures to mitigate cross-dynamics interference and optimizing data sampling are key areas for improvement.
- **Planning Compute Time**: Latent Noise Optimization (LNO) requires backpropagating gradients through all streaming rollout steps, causing computational costs to climb over longer horizons. Faster generative parameterizations such as Flow Maps could help enable online, real-time control.

sections.heading: Unified 3D Particle Generation Unites Simulation and Robot Control
sections.summary: GPWM unifies dynamics from rigid bodies to cloth under a shared particle and rigid-body representation, achieving exceptional long-horizon rollout stability via Diffusion Forcing. By leveraging a learned interaction prior, it opens a powerful new model-based route to solving contact-rich robotic manipulation without goal-specific policies.
sections.details: GPWM introduces a 3D particle world model for physical prediction and contact-rich planning. Combining a multi-resolution spatiotemporal Transformer with Diffusion Forcing enables stable rollouts far exceeding the 16-frame training window (up to 55x or more) without divergence. By capturing the coordinated motion of robots and objects as a generative prior, it presents a compelling framework that solves contact manipulation purely from goal specifications, without relying on reference trajectories or pre-trained reinforcement learning policies.

sections.heading: Appendix: Architecture Details, Training Setup, and Qualitative Comparisons
sections.summary: Details on the 4-level U-Net-style Transformer architecture, hybrid optimization with the Muon optimizer, and qualitative visual evaluations across domains.
sections.details:
### Network and Training Hyperparameters
The model features four resolution levels: coarse levels downsample anchors from the full particle set, with levels 3 and 4 serving as a bottleneck where 9 DiT blocks perform heavy computation. Rigid-body tokens bypass pooling and are preserved at all resolutions. Weight matrices are optimized using the Muon optimizer, while remaining parameters are trained with AdamW in a hybrid optimization scheme.

### Qualitative Visualizations
In long-horizon Free Fall and Dragging comparisons, baselines like PhysCtrl and PGND suffer from severe particle scattering, loss of volume, or shape collapse. In contrast, GPWM maintains crisp object volumes and rigid geometries throughout extensive rollouts.

captions.F6: Samples from each domain in the ParticleWorlds dataset. From top to bottom: free fall, deformable dragging, garment folding, rod pushing, gripper pushing, cluttered pick-and-place, and multi-fingered hand cube rotation.
captions.F7: Prediction comparison on unseen geometries in Free Fall. Compared to ground truth (GT), GPWM (Ours) preserves object shapes after multiple-body collisions without divergence, achieving significantly lower position error than PhysCtrl and GNS.
captions.F9: Qualitative comparison in Deformable Dragging. When an unseen shape is pulled and released, PGND scatters particles and collapses, and PhysCtrl accumulates large tracking errors, while GPWM accurately tracks deformation and elastic recovery.

takeaways: Targeting 3D particles and rigid transformations directly rather than 2D video pixels preserves strict geometric consistency and physical contact dynamics.
Combining Diffusion Forcing (independent noise levels per frame) with streaming generation prevents autoregressive error buildup, enabling rollouts dozens of times longer than the training window.
Jointly generating robot and object motions allows planning in latent noise space rather than action space, easily solving contact-rich tasks that are notoriously difficult to explore.

A single Unified model with shared weights can learn vastly different regimes—rigid bodies, elastoplasticity, granular media, and cloth—often matching or outperforming specialized single-domain models given a scaled dataset.
limitations: Relies on the assumption that fully tracked 3D particles and object segmentation are provided upfront, depending on external vision pipelines for real-world perception.
Latent Noise Optimization (LNO) requires backpropagating gradients through the entire diffusion rollout, taking tens to hundreds of seconds and remaining far from real-time control.
The Unified model slightly lags behind specialist models in a few domains, indicating lingering cross-domain interference between heterogeneous dynamics.
